articles.title: Hanging a clause off a main clause

article_json.also_called: Subordination, subordinate clauses and subordinating conjunctions
article_json.one_line: This lets you put two ideas in one sentence and show the reader which of them is your main point.
article_json.short_answer: Start the second clause with a word like *when*, *because* or *although*. At the front it takes a comma: *Because the line closed, journeys got longer.*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I join two ideas into one sentence without losing the main point?

body.text: One idea can lean on another instead of standing beside it
Two short sentences give both ideas the same weight. Often you do not want that. You want one idea to be the point and the other to be the setting, the reason or the condition for it.
So English lets you take one clause and hang it off the other. The hanging clause cannot stand alone, and that is the signal: it is background, and the clause it hangs on is the news.

body.gloss: hanging a clause off a main clause

show_first.text: Because the towpath flooded, the Verdon race was cancelled.
The council rebuilt the pier after the storm damaged it.
Although the fare rose, passenger numbers held up.

body.name_line: Joining two clauses this way is called **subordination**.
body.anchor_line: Cover the marked part in each one and a whole sentence is still standing. Cover the other part and nothing is.

body.text: Eight jobs a hanging clause does, and the words that start it

body.caption: The joining word tells the reader what job the clause is doing.
rows: Once the survey ended, work restarted.
Buses stop where the two roads meet.
The gate is shut because the ice is thick.
They moved the stop so that buses could turn.
The fog was so thick that ferries stopped.
Although fares rose, demand held up.
what has to be true first
Take a torch in case the lights fail.
She spoke as if the decision was final.
footnotes: Each row has its own article with the complete word list. This table is the map.
*if*-sentences have their own rules about which verb form goes in each half.

body.one_line: An *if*-clause hangs on a main clause like the others, but the two halves also have to agree about how real the situation is: *If the fund closes, the site goes back on the market.* The full story is in [th_conditionals_real].

body.lead_in: The same two facts, joined eight different ways. Only the joining word changes.

items.text: When the depot moved, the morning run got shorter.
items.gloss: The move happened, and after it the run was shorter.

items.text: Because the depot moved, the morning run got shorter.
items.gloss: The move is the reason the run is shorter.

items.text: Although the depot moved, the morning run got longer.
items.gloss: You would expect the move to shorten the run. It did not.

items.text: If the depot moves, the morning run will get shorter.
items.gloss: The move has not happened yet. It might.

body.so_what: One word decides whether the first fact is a time, a reason, a surprise or a condition.

body.caption: The hanging clause is the setting. The main clause is the news.

body.text: Front position takes a comma. End position usually does not
Put a comma after a hanging clause that comes first. Leave the comma out when the same clause comes last.

body.lead_in: The same sentence twice, with the hanging clause moved. Watch the comma appear and disappear.

items.text: After the ferry stopped running, the coast road filled up.
items.gloss: The ferry stopped first. Then the road filled up.

items.text: The coast road filled up after the ferry stopped running.
items.gloss: Same two events, same order, no comma needed.

items.text: Until the new bridge opens, lorries have to go round.
items.gloss: The detour lasts up to the day the bridge opens.

items.text: Lorries have to go round until the new bridge opens.
items.gloss: Same detour, same end point.

body.so_what: Moving the clause to the front changes the punctuation and the emphasis, and nothing else.

body.text: Fronting the clause is worth doing. It varies how your sentences start, and it puts the background before the point, which is where a reader wants it. Two or three fronted clauses in a paragraph is plenty.
What goes wrong

body.wrong: Because the Norland line was closed for repairs. Commuters drove instead.
body.right: Because the Norland line was closed for repairs, commuters drove instead.
body.why_it_happens: The first group of words is long and has a subject and a verb in it, so it feels like a sentence. *Because* is what stops it standing alone, and a full stop leaves it with nothing to lean on.
body.smallest_fix: Change the full stop to a comma and join it to the clause that follows.

body.wrong: Although the scheme cost more than planned, but the council approved it.
body.right: Although the scheme cost more than planned, the council approved it.
body.why_it_happens: Several languages mark both halves of a contrast, so both words feel necessary. English marks the relationship once. Keeping *although* and *but* together says the same thing twice.
body.smallest_fix: Delete one of them. Keep *although* and drop *but*, or keep *but* and drop *although*.

body.wrong: Because the fare doubled, more people took the train.
body.right: Although the fare doubled, more people took the train.
body.why_it_happens: *Because* and *although* both sit in the same slot, so they feel interchangeable. *Because* says the first fact caused the second; *although* says the first fact should have stopped it.
body.smallest_fix: Ask whether the second half is the expected result or the surprising one. Surprising takes *although*.

also_known_as: you can't begin a sentence with because
because always goes in the middle
body.truth: You can, and it is normal written English. *Because the tide was high, the crossing was cancelled.* is correct. The real problem is a sentence that has only the *because* part in it and no main clause.
body.what_to_do: Start with *because* whenever the reason belongs first. Then check that the sentence also contains a clause that could stand on its own.

body.mechanism: Chinese regularly marks a concession at both ends, with a word like *suirán* in the first clause and *dànshì* in the second.
body.wrong: Although the site is small, but it holds two hundred people.
body.right: Although the site is small, it holds two hundred people.
body.fix: Mark the relationship once in English. Use *although* or *but*, never both.

article_json.also_called: Defining (restrictive) relative clauses, and the zero relative
article_json.one_line: This lets you point at one noun out of many and tell the reader exactly which one you are talking about.
article_json.short_answer: Put *who*, *which* or *that* straight after the noun and add no commas. *The residents who objected were not consulted.*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say which person or which thing I mean, inside one sentence?

body.text: Narrowing a noun down to the one you mean
*The residents* could be all of them. *The residents who objected* is a smaller group. The extra words do a job: they cut the noun down until only the ones you mean are left.
That is the whole point of this structure. Take the extra words away and the reader no longer knows who or what you are talking about, so the sentence loses information.

body.gloss: an extra piece that tells you which noun you mean

show_first.text: The bus that stops outside the clinic runs twice an hour.
Students who live off campus pay a travel levy.
The report which the panel rejected has been rewritten.

body.name_line: That extra piece is called a **relative clause**.
body.anchor_line: It sits right behind the noun it belongs to, and it starts with *who*, *which* or *that*.

body.gloss: narrowing down which one / just adding extra information

show_first.text: Roads that flood every winter are being resurfaced.
The clinic, which opened in March, already has a waiting list.
Applicants who miss the deadline go on a reserve list.

body.name_line: A clause that narrows the noun down is **defining**; one that only adds a comment is **non-defining**.
body.anchor_line: The first and third examples pick out some roads and some applicants. The second one just tells you something extra about a clinic you already knew.

body.text: How to build one: the noun, the joining word, then the clause

body.caption: The noun in front decides the joining word, not the meaning of the sentence.
rows: the surveyor who wrote the report
the survey which took two years
the depot where the buses are kept
the week when the line was shut
the reason why the trial stopped
footnotes: *that* works for people and for things, and only in this kind of clause.
No comma goes in front of any of these.

body.lead_in: The same main sentence four times, with a different noun narrowed down each time.

items.text: The tenants who signed early kept the old rent.
items.gloss: Only the early signers kept it. The others did not.

items.text: The route that avoids the level crossing takes ten minutes longer.
items.gloss: One of the routes goes round. That one is slower.

items.text: The hall where the classes run has no lift.
items.gloss: One particular hall is meant, and it is hard to reach.

items.text: Countries that depend on tourism lost the most income.
items.gloss: Some countries depend on tourism. Those ones lost most.

body.so_what: In each one, deleting the marked part leaves a sentence that no longer says which tenants, which route, which hall or which countries.

body.text: When you can leave the joining word out
Look at what comes straight after the joining word. If a new subject comes next, you can drop the word. If a verb comes next, you cannot, because the joining word is doing the subject's job.
Leave out *who*, *which* or *that* when a new subject follows it. Keep it when a verb follows it.

body.lead_in: The first two can drop the joining word. The last two cannot. Watch what follows it.

items.text: The flat (that) we viewed on Tuesday has already gone.
items.gloss: A flat you looked at is no longer available.

items.text: The figures (which) the panel published are three years old.
items.gloss: The published figures are out of date.

items.text: The engineer who signed the certificate has retired.
items.gloss: One engineer signed it, and that person no longer works there.

items.text: A charge that applies to every vehicle is easier to explain.
items.gloss: A charge with no exceptions is simpler to describe.

body.so_what: A subject after the joining word means you can drop it. A verb after it means you cannot.

body.caption: Three slots: the noun, the joining word, then the rest of the clause.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The problem which the council is trying to solve it has no cheap answer.
body.right: The problem which the council is trying to solve has no cheap answer.
body.why_it_happens: Several languages require a pronoun inside the clause as well as the joining word. In English the joining word already is the object, so a second one names the same thing twice.
body.smallest_fix: Delete the extra *it*, *him* or *them* inside the clause.

body.wrong: Staff which work night shifts get an extra allowance.
body.right: Staff who work night shifts get an extra allowance.
body.why_it_happens: *Which* feels like the general-purpose word, and *staff* looks like a thing rather than a group of people. In careful writing *which* is not used for people.
body.smallest_fix: Use *who* whenever the noun is people. *That* is also correct here.

body.wrong: The inspector visited the site found two faults.
body.right: The inspector who visited the site found two faults.
body.why_it_happens: You have already seen that the joining word can be dropped, so it starts to look optional everywhere. Here it is the subject of *visited*, and dropping it leaves the sentence with two verbs and nothing to hold them apart.
body.smallest_fix: Put *who* or *that* back in front of the verb.

body.heard: Use *that* for things and *who* for people, and never mix them.
body.truth: *That* is used for people as well: *the engineer that signed it* is standard English. What *that* cannot do is follow a comma, and it cannot follow a preposition.
body.what_to_do: Use *who* for people if you prefer it; it always sounds right. Use *that* freely for things, and know that it is correct for people too.

body.mechanism: Arabic relative clauses normally keep a pronoun inside the clause that refers back to the noun, so both the joining word and the pronoun are present.
body.wrong: The report which I read it last week is out of date.
body.right: The report which I read last week is out of date.
body.fix: Delete the pronoun inside the clause. English uses the joining word alone.

articles.title: Adding extra information, and the comma that does it

article_json.also_called: Non-defining (non-restrictive) relative clauses, and the sentential relative
article_json.one_line: This lets you drop a comment about something into the middle of a sentence without starting a new one.
article_json.short_answer: Put commas both sides and never use *that*. *The Marlow depot, which closed in 2019, is being redeveloped.*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: When do I put commas round a *who* or *which* clause, and what do they change?

body.text: Two commas change what the sentence is true of
A relative clause with no commas narrows the noun down. The same clause with commas round it does not narrow anything. It comments on a noun the reader has already picked out.

So the commas are not decoration and they are not a rhythm choice. They tell the reader whether the clause is doing identifying work or not, and a reader who trusts them will read two different meanings.
How to build one: commas, and never *that*

body.caption: Four differences, and all four follow from one question about meaning.
rows: Can I drop the joining word?
Can it point at the whole clause?
footnotes: If the clause ends in the middle of the sentence, the second comma is not optional.

body.lead_in: One comment dropped into four different sentences. The commas hold it in place.

items.text: The Sandmouth ferry, which runs hourly, takes forty minutes.
items.gloss: There is one ferry. It runs hourly and the crossing is forty minutes.

items.text: Our tutor, who trained as an engineer, marks the diagrams himself.
items.gloss: One tutor is meant, and his background explains the marking.

items.text: The 2019 review, which nobody published, recommended closing two sites.
items.gloss: There was one review that year. It stayed unpublished.

items.text: Brackenfield College, where my sister studied, has doubled in size.
items.gloss: The college is already identified. The clause adds a personal detail.

body.so_what: In every one, deleting the marked part leaves a sentence that still names exactly the same thing.

body.text: Is this clause telling me which one, or just adding to it?

body.question: If I delete this clause, do I still know exactly who or what is meant?

options.label: no commas
options.use_it_when: Deleting the clause would leave the reader unsure which one you mean. The clause is doing identifying work.
options.example: Roads that flood every winter are being resurfaced.

options.label: commas both sides
options.use_it_when: The noun is already identified, by a name or by the situation, and the clause only adds a comment.
options.example: The coast road, which floods every winter, is being resurfaced.

a.text: The engineers who had worked on the bridge were interviewed.
a.means: Only some of the engineers worked on the bridge. Those ones were interviewed.

b.text: The engineers, who had worked on the bridge, were interviewed.
b.means: All of them worked on the bridge, and all of them were interviewed.

a.text: Countries that rely on tourism suffered the sharpest fall.
a.means: Some countries rely on tourism. Those ones fell hardest.

b.text: Countries, which rely on tourism, suffered the sharpest fall.
b.means: Every country in the world relies on tourism, which is not true.

a.text: My cousin who lives in Norland runs a bike shop.
a.means: You have more than one cousin. This is the Norland one.

b.text: My cousin, who lives in Norland, runs a bike shop.
b.means: You have one cousin, and he happens to live in Norland.

a.text: The samples which were stored below freezing survived.
a.means: Some samples were kept cold. Only those ones survived.

b.text: The samples, which were stored below freezing, survived.
b.means: All the samples were kept cold, and all of them survived.

body.deciding_factor: Delete the clause and read what is left. If you still know exactly which one is meant, the clause takes commas.
body.trap: You were taught the commas as a punctuation habit, so you add them where the sentence sounds like it needs a pause — and the pause has nothing to do with it.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. The comma version is the single cheapest way to add a comment in Task 2 writing without starting a new sentence.

body.text: *Which* can also point back at the whole sentence
After a comma, *which* does not have to point at a noun. It can point back at everything you have just said. That is how you add a consequence without a new sentence.

body.lead_in: In each one, *which* points at the whole first half, not at any single noun.

items.text: Fees rose twice in one year, which few families had budgeted for.
items.gloss: The rises were unplanned for. The families had budgeted for one at most.

marks.span: , which few families had budgeted for

items.text: The line closed for eight weeks, which pushed traffic onto the coast road.
items.gloss: The closure sent the cars somewhere else.

marks.span: , which pushed traffic onto the coast road

items.text: Nobody checked the readings, which meant the fault ran for a month.
items.gloss: Because of the missed checks, the fault lasted much longer.

marks.span: , which meant the fault ran for a month

body.so_what: You can attach a consequence to a whole statement with one comma and one word.

body.text: Use commas when the noun is already identified. Never use *that* after a comma, and never drop the joining word.

body.lead_in: Three sentences where the noun is already fixed, so the commas are the only correct choice.

items.text: Ashfield Hospital, which opened in 1974, is due for replacement.
items.gloss: One named hospital, with its opening date added.

items.text: My supervisor, who marks the drafts, is away until Monday.
items.gloss: One supervisor, and the reason her absence matters.

items.text: The final report, which ran to two hundred pages, arrived in May.
items.gloss: There was one final report, and it was long.

body.so_what: None of these clauses tells you which one. Each one comments on something already fixed.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The tunnel, which reopened in March has cut ten minutes off the journey.
body.right: The tunnel, which reopened in March, has cut ten minutes off the journey.
body.why_it_happens: The first comma feels like the pause before the extra information, and once the extra information is finished the sentence seems to run on by itself. The clause needs closing as well as opening.
body.smallest_fix: Put the second comma in, straight after the last word of the clause.

body.wrong: The Verdon wharf, that has stood empty since 2015, is up for sale.
body.right: The Verdon wharf, which has stood empty since 2015, is up for sale.
body.why_it_happens: *That* is the word you reach for first because it works everywhere else. It is the one relative word that cannot follow a comma.
body.smallest_fix: Change *that* to *which* for a thing, or to *who* for a person.

body.wrong: Employees, who work from home, are not entitled to the travel allowance.
body.right: Employees who work from home are not entitled to the travel allowance.
body.why_it_happens: The commas were added for rhythm. With them the sentence says that every employee works from home and none of them gets the allowance, which is not what was meant.
body.smallest_fix: Take both commas out. The clause is picking out one group of employees.

body.what_varies: Whether *which* may start a clause that has no commas.

option_a.label: British usage
option_a.form: *which* is free in both kinds of clause
option_a.example: The route which avoids the crossing is slower.

option_b.label: much American editing
option_b.form: *that* for the no-comma kind, *which* only after a comma
option_b.example: The route that avoids the crossing is slower.

body.why_this_default: *That* is accepted in both traditions, so it never draws a correction. This is a house choice for our examples, not a rule of English.

body.heard: Put a comma before *which* and no comma before *that*.
body.truth: That describes what usually happens; it does not tell you what to do. The comma is decided by whether the clause tells the reader which one you mean, and the joining word follows from that.
body.what_to_do: Decide the comma first, by deleting the clause and seeing whether you still know which one is meant. Then pick the joining word: never *that* after a comma.

body.headline: Delete the clause. If you still know which one, use commas.

article_json.also_called: Possessive, prepositional and quantified relative clauses; *whom*
article_json.one_line: This gives you the three relative structures that carry the most information for the least risk.
article_json.short_answer: Use *whose* for people and things alike. Put the preposition at the end in speech, in front of *which* in formal writing.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say *the company whose accounts failed* or *the panel to which she reported*?
article_json.risk_note: *Whom* is safe straight after a preposition and risky anywhere else. If you are unsure, use *who* or move the preposition to the end.

body.text: Three things a plain *who* or *which* cannot do
*Who* and *which* cover most relative clauses. Three jobs need something more: saying that something belongs to the noun, attaching a small placing word, and counting part of a group.
All three are worth having. They pack a second fact into a noun group instead of a second sentence, and none of them is hard to build.
*Whose* works for things, not only for people
Use *whose* whenever the next thing you say belongs to the noun. It works for people, organisations, animals and objects.

body.lead_in: Four nouns of four different kinds, all taking *whose*.

items.text: The tutor whose office is on the top floor takes Friday sessions.
items.gloss: One tutor is meant, identified by where he works.

items.text: A company whose margins had collapsed cannot fund the repairs.
items.gloss: The firm has no money left, so the work cannot happen.

items.text: The building whose roof was rebuilt is now the archive.
items.gloss: One building had a new roof, and it holds the archive.

items.text: That's the flat whose balcony overlooks the canal.
items.gloss: One particular flat has the view over the water.

body.so_what: *Whose* never changed shape, and none of these four nouns is a person.

body.text: The preposition goes at the end, or in front of *which*

body.caption: Both are correct. The front version is the formal one.
rows: the scheme which they objected to
the scheme to which they objected
the officer to whom she reported
footnotes: *that* cannot follow a preposition: never *the scheme to that they objected*.
The joining word cannot be dropped when the preposition is in front of it.

body.lead_in: The same fact three ways, from most formal to most spoken.

items.text: The panel to which the complaint was sent has not replied.
items.gloss: The complaint went to a panel, and no answer has come.

items.text: The panel which the complaint was sent to has not replied.
items.gloss: Same panel, same silence.

items.text: The panel the complaint was sent to hasn't replied.
items.gloss: Same again, as you would say it out loud.

body.so_what: All three are correct English. Only the register changes.

body.text: Counting part of a group: *many of whom*, *some of which*
After a comma you can start the clause with a counting word and *of*. It lets you say something about part of the group you have just named, in the same sentence.

body.lead_in: Each one names a group, then says something about part of it.

items.text: The trust owns nine buildings, three of which are empty.
items.gloss: Nine buildings in total, and three have nobody in them.

items.text: Two hundred residents replied, most of whom opposed the charge.
items.gloss: Most of the people who answered were against it.

items.text: We looked at four sites, none of which had road access.
items.gloss: Not one of the four could be reached by lorry.

items.text: The survey covered six wards, half of which reported flooding.
items.gloss: Three of the six wards had water problems.

body.so_what: *Whom* is the form after *of*, and this is the one place it is easy to get right.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The company which its accounts were rejected has appealed.
body.right: The company whose accounts were rejected has appealed.
body.why_it_happens: *Whose* looks like a word for people only, so a possessive pronoun goes in instead. That leaves two joining devices doing one job.
body.smallest_fix: Replace *which its* with *whose*.

body.wrong: The fund from that the grants are paid closes in April.
body.right: The fund from which the grants are paid closes in April.
body.why_it_happens: *That* works in most no-comma clauses, so it feels safe here too. It is the one relative word that cannot sit behind a preposition.
body.smallest_fix: Use *which*, or move the small word to the end: *the fund that the grants are paid from*.

body.wrong: The surveyor whom signed the report has left.
body.right: The surveyor who signed the report has left.
body.why_it_happens: *Whom* sounds more careful, so it gets used wherever the sentence feels formal. It cannot be the subject of the verb inside the clause.
body.smallest_fix: Use *who* when a verb follows straight away. Keep *whom* for right after a preposition or *of*.

body.what_varies: Whether the small placing word goes in front of *which* or at the end.

option_b.label: speech and ordinary writing
option_b.example: the archive which the maps are kept in

body.why_this_default: The end position is correct in every register and never sounds stiff. This is a house choice for our examples, not a rule of English.

body.heard: *Which* can never start a defining clause, so always write *that*.
also_known_as: that for defining, which for non-defining
body.truth: That is an editing convention, followed closely in much American publishing and loosely elsewhere. In British usage *the route which avoids the crossing* is standard. What always matters is the comma, not the choice of word.
body.what_to_do: Use *that* in no-comma clauses if you want a form nobody can object to. Never use it after a comma, and never after a preposition.

articles.title: Cutting a *which* clause down to a phrase

article_json.also_called: Reduced relative clauses: participial and infinitival postmodification
article_json.one_line: This lets you say the same thing in four words instead of eight, without losing any information.
article_json.short_answer: Delete the joining word and *be*. *The changes which were introduced in 2019* becomes *the changes introduced in 2019.*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I shorten *the people who are living nearby* to *the people living nearby*?

body.text: The same information, in half the words

*The residents who are living within walking distance* and *the residents living within walking distance* say exactly the same thing. The second one is shorter, and the words it drops carry no meaning of their own.
This is where dense academic noun groups come from. It also runs the other way: when a shortened phrase confuses you, put the joining word and *be* back in and read it as a full clause.
Delete the joining word and *be*, and see what is left

body.caption: What is left behind tells you which of the three cuts you have made.
rows: the staff who are working nights

body.text: Setting one event against another in time
A time clause fixes one event against another. *The road flooded* is a fact. *When the tide turned, the road flooded* tells you what the road was waiting for.
Each joining word says something different about the order and the overlap. That is the choice you are making, and the words are a small closed set.

body.deciding_factor: If a describing word or an amount word can sit between *so* and *that*, you are naming an outcome. If not, you are naming an aim.
body.trap: *So* and *so that* look like the same word with an extra piece, so they get used for each other — and that turns somebody's plan into a claim about what happened.
body.register_note: *So* alone for a result is fine in speech and slightly loose in an essay, where *therefore*, *as a result* and *consequently* carry it better.

body.text: *To* on its own already means *in order to*
Use *to* + verb for an aim when both halves have the same subject. Use *so that* + a modal when the subjects are different.

body.lead_in: Three aims, two subjects. Watch when *to* is enough and when it is not.
body.dimension: whether the two halves share a subject

items.text: The trust bought the wharf to stop it being sold for flats.
items.gloss: The trust bought it, and the trust wanted to stop the sale.

items.text: The trust bought the wharf so that the boatyard could stay.
items.gloss: The trust bought it, and the boatyard is what benefits.

items.text: I left early to catch the four o'clock ferry.
items.gloss: One person, one aim, one subject.

items.text: Signs were put up so as not to lose walkers on the marsh.
items.gloss: The signs are there to keep people from getting lost.

body.so_what: A different subject in the second half is what forces *so that*.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The line closed because of the tunnel was flooded.
body.right: The line closed because the tunnel was flooded.
body.why_it_happens: *Because* and *because of* mean the same thing, so the longer one feels safer. *Because of* takes a noun group; only *because* can take a whole clause.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *of*, or write *because of the flooding*.

body.wrong: They closed the towpath for repairing the culvert.
body.right: They closed the towpath to repair the culvert.
body.why_it_happens: Many languages use a word like *for* to mark an aim, so *for* plus the *-ing* form looks like the natural translation. English uses *to* + verb when a person has an aim.
body.smallest_fix: Replace *for* + *-ing* with *to* + verb.

body.wrong: The stop was moved so that buses turn more safely.
body.right: The stop was moved so that buses could turn more safely.
body.why_it_happens: The aim is about a real situation, so an ordinary present verb feels right. A *so that* clause names something that was wanted, and the modal is what carries that.
body.smallest_fix: Put *can*, *could*, *will* or *would* into the *so that* clause.

body.heard: *Due to* is the formal way of writing *because*, so use it in essays.
body.truth: *Due to* takes a noun group, exactly like *because of*. *Due to the wall moved* is not English. An older rule also restricted *due to* to positions after *be*, and many readers no longer apply it.
body.what_to_do: Use *because* before a clause and *due to* or *because of* before a noun group. Neither is more academic than the other.

body.headline: Reason looks back. Aim looks forward. Outcome is what happened.

article_json.one_line: This lets you put a fact that argues against you into your own sentence, and still keep your point.
article_json.short_answer: *Although* takes a clause. *Despite* takes a noun or an *-ing* form. *However* starts a new sentence.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: What comes after *although*, and what comes after *despite*?

body.text: Naming the fact that argues against your point
A strong argument names the fact on the other side and then says why it does not settle the matter. That move needs one of these words, and it is worth more than any other joining word in an essay.
Two different jobs hide inside the same word list. One says two facts are in tension. The other says two things are simply different. Mixing them up changes what you are claiming.
What follows the word decides which word you can use

body.caption: Pick the word by looking at what you want to write after it.
rows: Although the fare rose, demand held up.
Rural sites lost staff, whereas urban ones grew.
Despite the higher fare, demand held up.
Despite the fact that fares rose, demand held up.
Fares rose, but demand held up.
Fares rose. However, demand held up.
footnotes: *However* is not a joining word. It cannot hold two clauses together on its own.
*Though* at the end of a sentence is spoken English only: *It's dear, though.*

body.lead_in: One pair of facts, written five ways. Watch what changes after the marked word.

items.text: Although the levy was unpopular, the council kept it.
items.gloss: People disliked it and it stayed.

items.text: Despite its unpopularity, the council kept the levy.
items.gloss: Same two facts, with a noun after the marked word.

items.text: Despite being unpopular, the levy stayed in place.
items.gloss: Same again, with an *-ing* form instead of a noun.

items.text: The levy was unpopular. However, the council kept it.
items.gloss: Same two facts split into two sentences.

items.text: It was unpopular, but they kept it anyway.
items.gloss: The spoken version of the same thing.

body.so_what: Every one is correct. What changed each time is the shape of the words that follow.

body.text: Tension, or just a difference?

body.question: Are the two facts fighting each other, or are they simply not the same?

options.label: *although* — tension
options.use_it_when: The first fact would normally stop the second one from being true, and it does not. You are conceding something.
options.example: Although the clinic was rebuilt, waiting times did not fall.

options.label: *whereas* — a plain difference
options.use_it_when: You are setting two things beside each other and reporting how they differ. Nothing surprising is being claimed.
options.example: Waiting times fell in Ashfield, whereas they rose in Norland.

a.text: Although rural clinics lost staff, urban ones grew.
a.means: You are treating the urban growth as surprising, given the rural losses.

b.text: Rural clinics lost staff, whereas urban ones grew.
b.means: You are reporting a straight difference between two kinds of place.

a.text: Although older workers value security, they change jobs often.
a.means: The job-changing goes against what you would expect from them.

b.text: Older workers value security, whereas younger ones rank pay first.
b.means: Two groups want different things. Neither is surprising.

a.text: Even though the site flooded twice, the works finished on time.
a.means: The floods should have caused a delay and did not.

b.text: The site flooded twice, while the depot stayed dry all winter.
b.means: Two places, two different winters. No tension.

body.deciding_factor: Ask whether a reader would say *and yet* at the join. If yes, use *although*. If they would say *and on the other hand*, use *whereas*.
body.trap: Both words sit in the same slot in the sentence, so they feel like style choices. The choice tells the reader whether you are surrendering a point or comparing two things.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. A sentence that opens *While …* and then makes your point is the single most useful essay shape in this group.

body.text: Use *although* before a clause and *despite* before a noun group. Mark the contrast once, never twice.

body.lead_in: Three sentences, each marking the contrast exactly once.

items.text: Although the survey cost more than planned, it was worth doing.
items.gloss: The overspend did not make it a waste.

items.text: Despite the extra cost, the survey was worth doing.
items.gloss: Same judgement, with a noun group after the marker.

items.text: The survey cost more than planned. It was still worth doing.
items.gloss: Two sentences, with *still* carrying the contrast.

body.so_what: None of them uses two contrast words for one contrast.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: Despite the cost was high, the scheme went ahead.
body.right: Despite the high cost, the scheme went ahead.
body.why_it_happens: *Despite* and *although* both mark a contrast, so they look like the same kind of word. *Despite* is a placing word: it takes a noun group, not a clause with its own verb.
body.smallest_fix: Turn the clause into a noun group, or change *despite* to *although*.

body.wrong: Although the flat is small, but the rent is reasonable.
body.right: Although the flat is small, the rent is reasonable.
body.why_it_happens: Several languages mark both halves of a contrast, so leaving one half unmarked feels incomplete. English marks the relationship once.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *but*, or delete *although* and keep *but*.

body.wrong: The cost was high, however the scheme went ahead.
body.right: The cost was high. However, the scheme went ahead.
body.why_it_happens: *However* means the same as *but*, so it goes into the same slot. *However* cannot hold two clauses together, so the comma is left doing a job it cannot do.
body.smallest_fix: Use a full stop or a semicolon before *however*, and a comma after it.

body.heard: *While* and *whereas* are just formal words for *although*.
body.truth: *While* does both jobs, and *whereas* does only one: it sets two things side by side. *Whereas the fare rose, demand held up* asks the reader to feel a tension that *whereas* does not carry. *Whereas* also never means time.
body.what_to_do: Use *whereas* for a plain difference between two things. Use *although* or *even though* when the first fact should have blocked the second.

body.headline: Clause after *although*. Noun group after *despite*. New sentence for *however*.

article_json.one_line: This lets you say how something was done, how it compares with something else, and what the one exception is.
article_json.short_answer: *As if* + clause for how it seems. *Than* + clause for a comparison. *The more … the more* for two things moving together.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say *he talks as if he owned the place* or *the longer we wait, the worse it gets*?

body.text: Four small clause types that carry a lot

These four are usually left out of course books, and each one saves a whole sentence. They say how something happened, how two things compare, how they move together, and where the one exception lies.
How it was done, and how it seemed

body.caption: *As* reports a real way of doing something; *as if* reports an impression.
rows: in the way that was agreed or expected
The panel voted as the rules require.
Fit the bracket the way the diagram shows.
it looks like this, and it may not be so
The engine sounds as if a belt is slipping.
the same as *as if*, in speech
It looks like the meeting is off.
footnotes: *Like* before a clause is normal speech and is best avoided in an essay.

body.text: After *as if* you have a choice. A present form says the impression might be true. A past form says you know it is not, even though you are talking about now.

body.lead_in: The same impression, once as possible and once as known to be false.

items.text: The pump sounds as if it is running dry.
items.gloss: It may really have no water in it.

items.text: He talks as if he owned the whole yard.
items.gloss: He does not own it, and everyone knows that.

items.text: The figures look as though they were copied twice.
items.gloss: You suspect a double entry, and you are not asserting it.

body.so_what: The past form is not about past time here. It marks the impression as untrue.

body.text: Comparing with a clause, not just a word
After *than* and after *as … as*, you can put a whole clause. Leave out any words the reader can supply.

body.lead_in: Three comparisons where a clause follows, not a single word.

items.text: The works cost more than the trust had budgeted for.
items.gloss: The bill came in above the planned figure.

marks.span: than the trust had budgeted for

items.text: Take-up was as strong as the pilot study had predicted.
items.gloss: The forecast matched what actually happened.

marks.span: as the pilot study had predicted

items.text: It took longer than we thought.
items.gloss: The job ran over the time you expected.

body.so_what: Each clause leaves out the repeated part, and the sentence is still complete.

body.text: Two things that move together: *the more … the more*
This shape links two changes. Both halves start with *the* and a comparing word, and the first half is the one that drives the other.

body.lead_in: Three pairs of changes moving together. Both halves carry *the*.

items.text: The longer the repair takes, the more the diversion costs.
items.gloss: A slow repair means a dearer diversion.

items.text: The higher the fare, the fewer people use the line.
items.gloss: Dearer tickets push passengers away.

items.text: The sooner you book, the cheaper it is.
items.gloss: Early booking saves money.

body.so_what: Both halves need *the*, and neither half is a full ordinary sentence.

body.text: Naming the one exception

body.lead_in: Three ways to name the single thing that does not fit:
items: *except that* + clause: *The flat is ideal, except that the boiler is old.*
*apart from the fact that* + clause: *Apart from the fact that it floods, the site is good.*
*other than* + noun: *Other than the boiler, everything works.*

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The longer the repair takes, more the diversion costs.
body.right: The longer the repair takes, the more the diversion costs.
body.why_it_happens: The second half looks like an ordinary clause, so the little word in front of *more* seems unnecessary. Both halves of this shape need *the*, and it is what holds the two changes together.
body.smallest_fix: Put *the* in front of the comparing word in the second half.

body.wrong: He behaves as if he is the site manager, but he left last year.
body.right: He behaves as if he were the site manager, but he left last year.
body.why_it_happens: The behaviour is happening now, so a present form feels right. When you know the impression is false, English uses a past form to say so.
body.smallest_fix: Change *is* to *was* or *were*. Both are used; *were* is the careful written form.

body.wrong: The works cost twice more than the trust had budgeted for.
body.right: The works cost twice as much as the trust had budgeted for.
body.why_it_happens: *Twice* and *more* both point at a bigger amount, so putting them together seems to make the point stronger. A multiple takes *as … as*, not *more than*.
body.smallest_fix: Use *twice as much as*, or drop *twice* and keep *more than*.

body.heard: *Like* is wrong before a clause, so always write *as*.
body.truth: *Like the diagram shows* is normal spoken English and has been for a long time. It is a register split, not an error: *as* is the choice in careful writing, and some readers do object to *like* there.
body.what_to_do: Say *like* freely in speech. Write *as* or *as if* in an essay, where the objection is common enough to matter.

body.headline: *As if* for impressions, *than* for comparisons, *the … the* for pairs.

article_json.one_line: This gives you the four shapes a verb takes when it is not the one carrying the time in the sentence.

body.text: Only one verb in a sentence carries the time
In *The panel decided to publish the figures*, only *decided* says when. *Publish* says what, and it takes a shape with no time on it at all.
There are four such shapes, and knowing which is which is what makes the verb-pattern lists usable. Each one has a name, and you will meet all four everywhere in this chapter.

show_first.text: The trust agreed to fund half the cost.
Nobody offered to check the readings.
She hopes to start the course in autumn.

body.anchor_line: It never changes shape, whoever the subject is and whenever the sentence happens.

show_first.text: The rules make every visitor sign in.
They let us use the north hall.
You should check the tide table first.

body.name_line: The same form with the *to* removed is called the **bare infinitive**.
body.anchor_line: It turns up after modal verbs, after *make* and *let*, and in a short closed list of other places.

body.gloss: the *-ing* form used as a noun: *swimming is cheap*

show_first.text: Replacing the culverts proved expensive.
They avoided answering the question.
Cycling to work saves an hour a day.

body.name_line: The *-ing* form standing where a noun could stand is called the **gerund**.
body.anchor_line: Swap the marked part for a plain noun like *the work* and the sentence still holds together.

body.gloss: a verb form used with a helper or as a describing word

show_first.text: The crew working on the span finish at six.
The figures published last week are wrong.
A leaking valve caused the whole shutdown.

body.name_line: An *-ing* or third form used to describe a noun is called a **participle**.
body.anchor_line: The *-ing* one says the noun is doing it; the third form says the noun is having it done to it.

body.caption: Every shape has a passive version except the two continuous ones.
footnotes: The two gaps are combinations English does not use. Nothing is missing by accident.
The negative goes in front of the whole thing, with no *do*: *not to write*, *not having written*.

items.text: The board agreed to review the contract in June.
items.gloss: A review was decided on for June.

items.text: The auditor made them review the contract again.
items.gloss: They had no choice about the second review.

items.text: Reviewing the contract took most of a week.
items.gloss: The job itself filled nearly a week.

items.text: The contract reviewed in June is the one we signed.
items.gloss: One of the versions is the signed one.

body.so_what: One verb, four shapes, and not one of them says when anything happened.

body.text: Where the form with no *to* is required
Use the bare form after a modal verb, after *do*, *make* and *let*, and after *had better* and *would rather*.

body.lead_in: The complete list of places the bare form is required:
items: after the modal verbs: *she must check the readings*
after *do*, *does* and *did*: *they didn't check the readings*
after *had better* and *would rather*: *you'd better check it*
after *make* and *let* with an object: *the rules make everyone sign in*
after *see*, *hear* and *watch* with an object: *I heard the pump stop*
after *help*, where *to* is optional: *she helped us carry it*
after *why* and *why not*: *why not check the archive?*

body.lead_in: Three sentences from that list, all with no *to* in sight.

items.text: The site rules make every driver report to the gate.
items.gloss: Reporting at the gate is compulsory for drivers.

items.text: We heard the generator cut out just after midnight.
items.gloss: The power went off and you heard the whole thing.

items.text: You'd better book the ferry before the weekend.
items.gloss: Leaving it later is risky.

body.so_what: In each one a *to* would be wrong, and nothing else in the sentence changes.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: Every driver must to report to the gate on arrival.
body.right: Every driver must report to the gate on arrival.
body.why_it_happens: Most verbs that take another verb use *to*, so *to* starts to look like part of the second verb. Modal verbs are the group that takes the bare form.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *to* after *must*, *can*, *should*, *may*, *might* and *will*.

body.wrong: The auditor made them to review the contract again.
body.right: The auditor made them review the contract again.
body.why_it_happens: *Force* and *get* both take *to* in this position, so *make* looks as though it should too. *Make* and *let* take the bare form.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *to* after *make* and *let*. Note that the passive of *make* puts it back: *they were made to review it*.

body.wrong: The figures publishing last week contain two errors.
body.right: The figures published last week contain two errors.
body.why_it_happens: The *-ing* form is the one most often practised, so it becomes the default describing form. The figures did not publish anything; somebody published them.
body.smallest_fix: Use the third form when the noun is on the receiving end of the action.

body.heard: The *-ing* form is the continuous tense, so it always means something is going on now.
body.truth: The *-ing* form does that job only when *be* is in front of it. On its own it is a noun-like form or a describing word: *cycling saves an hour*, *a leaking valve*. Neither of those is about this moment.
body.what_to_do: Look for *be* in front of the *-ing* form. Without it, the form is not saying anything about time.

articles.title: Which verbs take *-ing* and which take *to*

article_json.also_called: Verb + gerund, verb + *to*-infinitive, and the preposition rule
article_json.one_line: This tells you which of the two shapes a second verb takes, and why most of it has to be learned as a list.
article_json.short_answer: There is no rule that predicts it. Learn the verb with its shape: *avoid doing*, *agree to do*. After a preposition, always *-ing*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I know whether to write *enjoy swimming* or *enjoy to swim*?

body.text: There is one rule here, and the rest is a list
*Enjoy* takes *-ing*. *Want* takes *to*. Nothing in what those two verbs mean explains the difference, and no rule predicts it. The shape is a property of the first verb, like its spelling.
So this article gives you one real rule, two lists, and honest labelling of which is which. Hunting for a rule behind the lists costs weeks and finds nothing.
After any placing word, the verb takes *-ing*
After a preposition, a verb always takes the *-ing* form. There are no exceptions.

body.lead_in: Four different placing words, one form after all of them.

items.text: The trust succeeded in cutting the waiting list by half.
items.gloss: The list is half as long as it was.

items.text: She is interested in working on the coastal survey.
items.gloss: The survey is the job she would like.

items.text: They left without signing the visitors' book.
items.gloss: Nobody wrote their names down on the way out.

items.text: I'm no good at reading those old maps.
items.gloss: The old maps defeat you.

body.so_what: The placing word decides the shape, and the meaning of the verb has nothing to do with it.

body.text: The *to* that is a placing word, not part of the verb
A small set of expressions ends in a *to* that is a placing word. The rule above still applies, so the verb after it takes *-ing*. This looks wrong to almost everybody the first time.

she is used to working outdoors
they objected to paying the surcharge
in addition to funding the survey
footnotes: The test is the whole answer: put a noun after the *to*. If it works, the verb takes *-ing*.

Fixed phrases in the first group: *it's no use*, *there's no point in*, *be worth*, *can't help*, *can't stand*.

items.gloss: New handrails will have to wait.

items.text: The contractor failed to notify the site office.
items.gloss: Nobody in the office was told.

items.text: We spent three weeks checking the archive by hand.
items.gloss: The manual check took three weeks.

items.text: They can't afford to run two vans any more.
items.gloss: One van is all the money will cover.

body.so_what: You cannot work any of these out from the meaning. Each verb brings its own shape with it.

body.label: Three groups where both shapes are correct

items.text: *begin*, *start*, *continue* and *cease* take either shape with no change of meaning.
items.example: The render began cracking last winter.

items.text: Avoid two *-ing* forms in a row. When the first verb is already an *-ing* form, use *to*.
items.example: The render is starting to crack along the sill.

items.text: *like*, *love*, *hate* and *prefer* take both. After *would*, only *to* is possible.
items.example: I'd like to see the figures before Friday.

body.stop_line: That is the whole list of free choices, apart from the ten verbs where the shape changes the meaning, which have their own article.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: I look forward to hear from the admissions office.
body.right: I look forward to hearing from the admissions office.
body.why_it_happens: *To* almost always comes in front of a plain verb, so *to hearing* looks like a mistake and gets corrected. Here *to* is a placing word, and a placing word takes the *-ing* form.
body.smallest_fix: Try putting a noun after the *to*. If *to the letter* works, write *to hearing*.

body.wrong: The council avoided to answer the question about costs.
body.right: The council avoided answering the question about costs.
body.why_it_happens: *To* is the shape most learners meet first, so it becomes the default second verb. *Avoid* is in the other list, and no meaning in the word tells you that.
body.smallest_fix: Check the verb against the list. *Avoid*, *enjoy*, *finish*, *suggest* and *deny* all take *-ing*.

body.wrong: The report suggests the council to build more housing.
body.right: The report suggests building more housing.
body.why_it_happens: *Advise*, *ask* and *tell* all take a person and then *to*, so *suggest* looks like it belongs with them. *Suggest* never takes a person plus *to*.
body.smallest_fix: Write *suggests building*, or *suggests that the council should build*.

body.heard: *-ing* is for things you enjoy, and *to* is for things you plan.
also_known_as: the meaning tells you which form
body.truth: It fits *enjoy* and *plan* and fails everywhere else. *Avoid*, *deny*, *risk* and *resent* are not about enjoyment, and they all take *-ing*. There is no meaning behind the split.
body.what_to_do: Learn each verb with its shape as one chunk, the way you learn a spelling. Keep the one real rule for placing words.

body.text: Two people, one clause
*The reform enabled councils to borrow directly.* One thing acts, another thing does the borrowing. English fits both into one clause by putting the second person straight after the first verb.
This is the workhorse pattern of academic writing. *Allow*, *enable*, *encourage*, *force* and *prevent* carry most causal claims a writer needs to make.
The three shapes, and which verbs take each

body.caption: The first verb decides whether a *to* appears in the middle.
rows: advise, allow, ask, enable, encourage, expect
The grant enabled the trust to reopen the wharf.
force, invite, order, permit, persuade, remind

teach, tell, urge, want, warn, would like
The tutor told us to hand in two drafts.
The rules make every visitor sign in.

prevent from, stop from, accuse of, blame for
Flooding prevented the crew from finishing.
footnotes: *Help* takes both: *helped us carry it* and *helped us to carry it* are equally correct.
*Make* puts the *to* back in the passive: *every visitor is made to sign in*.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The office wants that we submit the form by Friday.
body.right: The office wants us to submit the form by Friday.
body.why_it_happens: Most European and South Asian languages use a *that*-clause here, so it is the shape that comes to mind first. *Want* and *would like* do not take one in English.
body.smallest_fix: Replace *that we submit* with *us to submit*.

body.wrong: The warden let us to park behind the gate.
body.right: The warden let us park behind the gate.
body.why_it_happens: *Allow* and *permit* mean the same thing and both take *to*, so *let* looks like it should as well. *Let* and *make* take the bare form.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *to*. In formal writing, use *allowed us to park* instead.

body.wrong: I recommend you to read the second chapter first.
body.right: I recommend reading the second chapter first.
body.why_it_happens: *Advise* takes a person and then *to*, and *recommend* means almost the same, so the pattern gets carried across. *Recommend* and *suggest* do not take a person plus *to*.
body.smallest_fix: Write *recommend reading*, or *recommend that you read*.

body.heard: *Let* is informal, so use *allow* in writing and you will never be wrong.
also_known_as: never write let in an essay
body.truth: *Let* is ordinary English and is not an error anywhere. It is less formal than *allow*, and the two take different shapes, so swapping one for the other means changing the rest of the clause as well.
body.what_to_do: Prefer *allow … to* and *enable … to* in an essay. When you do write *let*, remember it takes no *to*.

body.text: Ten verbs where the shape is not a list item
For most verbs the shape of the second verb is just something you learn. For about ten verbs it is a real choice, because the two versions describe different events.
These are worth learning properly. Both versions are correct English, so nothing marks the error except the reader, who believes what you wrote.
Which one describes what actually happened?

body.question: Is the second verb the thing that follows, or the activity itself?

options.label: *to* + verb
options.use_it_when: The second verb is what comes next: a purpose, an intention, or a duty still ahead of you.
options.example: The crew stopped to eat at the halfway point.

options.label: the *-ing* form
options.use_it_when: The second verb is the activity itself, or something already done that you now remember or regret.
options.example: The crew stopped painting at four o'clock.

a.text: I remember locking the gate before we drove off.
a.means: You did lock it, and you can picture yourself doing it.

b.text: Please remember to lock the gate before you drive off.
b.means: The gate is still open. Locking it comes later.

a.text: The trust regrets appointing him as site manager.
a.means: He was appointed, and the trust is sorry it happened.

b.text: We regret to inform you that the bid was unsuccessful.
b.means: You are being told bad news right now.

a.text: If the meter sticks, try tapping the casing twice.
a.means: Tapping is an experiment. It may or may not fix it.

b.text: We tried to reach the site before the tide turned.
b.means: Getting there was hard, and you may not have managed it.

a.text: She went on describing the site for another hour.
a.means: She carried on with the same description.

b.text: She went on to describe the costs in detail.
b.means: She finished the first topic and moved to a new one.

a.text: The handrails need repainting before the season starts.
a.means: Somebody has to paint them. The handrails are not doing it.

b.text: We need to repaint the handrails before the season starts.
b.means: The painting is your job.

body.deciding_factor: *To* points forward to something not done yet. *-ing* points at the activity itself, or back at something already done.
body.trap: Both versions are correct English and neither one is ever underlined, so the mistake never gets found. The reader simply takes in the wrong event.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. *Need* + *-ing* for a passive meaning is commoner in British English; *need to be repainted* works in every variety.

branches.answer: Yes — you did the first thing in order to do the second

verdict.example: The crew stopped to eat at the halfway point.
verdict.why: *To* + verb always carries a forward-looking purpose.

branches.answer: No — the second verb is the activity itself

verdict.example: The crew stopped painting at four o'clock.
verdict.why: Here the second verb names what came to an end, not why.

body.wrong: After twenty years on site he finally stopped to smoke.
body.right: After twenty years on site he finally gave up smoking.
body.why_it_happens: *Stop to smoke* looks like the fuller, more careful version of *stop smoking*. It says he paused work in order to have a cigarette, which is the opposite of what was meant.
body.smallest_fix: Use *stopped smoking* for giving it up, or *gave up smoking*, which cannot be misread.

body.why_it_happens: The instruction is about the future, and the *-ing* form is the shape practised most often. *Remember* + *-ing* tells somebody they already did it.
body.smallest_fix: Use *to* + verb whenever the action has not happened yet.

body.heard: *Stop doing* and *stop to do* are the formal and informal versions of the same thing.
also_known_as: they mean the same, one is just politer
body.truth: They describe two different afternoons. *The crew stopped painting* means no more paint went on. *The crew stopped to paint* means they broke off something else so that they could paint.
